## RibbonShape

Anchor in `spec/ui/components/ribbon/index.pi`, declared as a `shape`, extending `Shape`.

### RibbonShape.description

Type: `string`. Overrides `Shape.description`.

A ribbon runs along the top of the window, using gpui-kit's Tab component with its default styling, borders, and spacing, only in the ThemeScope's colours. Nothing adds to or takes away from a tab's own borders or margins, so a tab's label never shifts as tabs open and close. Along the top of the commands, a line in the colour of the tabs' own side borders runs from the far left, beneath the project indicator and the rest of the left container, to the side border of the first open tab, and on from that tab's other side border to the next open tab or the far right. An open tab meets the commands beneath it with no line between them, its side borders running straight down to where the line picks up again. There is no other line there, not even a faint one at a fractional display scale.
A tab whose commands work on one of the chat input's modes, as the Code and Spec tabs do, takes that mode's colour: its label is in the mode's colour while the tab is closed, and while open, the tab is tinted with it instead and its label is the tab's own colour. Each such tab says more. Its tabs are, in order: Project, Code, Spec, Research, and Application. The window always opens on Project. Beneath the tabs, the selected tab's commands sit in groups. There is no raw output view and no toggle for one.

### RibbonShape.keyboard

<Alt+1> opens the first tab, <Alt+2> the second, and so on, through each tab in the order the tabs are shown, <Alt+5> opening Application. Each opens its tab alone, as clicking it does, and expands the ribbon first if it is collapsed. A number past the last tab does nothing. Like the ribbon's other shortcuts, they do nothing while an inset panel is open. A tab's tooltip doesn't give its shortcut, since a tab has no tooltip.

### RibbonShape.openingSeveralTabs

Clicking a tab opens it alone, as usual. Ctrl+clicking one (Cmd+click on macOS) opens it alongside whichever tabs are already open, or, if it is already open, closes it, so any number of tabs can be open at once. The last open tab can't be closed this way: Ctrl+clicking it leaves it open. Every open tab shows as selected.
The command area then holds the groups of every open tab side by side, in the order of the tabs rather than the order they were opened, with no divider between one tab's groups and the next, as between any groups. An open tab with no commands adds nothing, and "No commands yet" shows only when none of the open tabs has any. When the groups are wider than the window, the command area scrolls sideways. The command area stays the same height however many tabs are open.
Double-clicking a tab still collapses the ribbon, and expanding it again shows the same tabs open. Which tabs are open isn't kept between

#### Launches

the window always opens with only Project open.

### RibbonShape.leftContainer

At the left end of the bar, left of the tab bar itself rather than inside it, so the tab bar's own padding and bottom line don't reach it, sits the left container. It holds, in order, the project indicator, the collapse chevron, and the activity spinner, and can hold other things after them. It is the same whether the ribbon is expanded, beside the tabs, or collapsed, leading the row of primary commands.
It runs from the top of the bar down to the line along its bottom, never over it, so it is the same height expanded and collapsed. Everything in it is vertically centred in that height, with no gap between one thing and the next and no padding around them: each thing's own size is all the room it takes. The container shrinks to fit what it holds, and when it holds nothing, it isn't there at all.

### RibbonShape.rightContainer

At the right end of the bar, right of the tabs, or of the primary commands when the ribbon is collapsed, sits the right container. It holds nothing yet, and can hold other things. It lays out what it holds as the left container does: vertically centred, with no gap between things and no padding around them, shrinking to fit, and not there at all while it holds nothing, as it is now.

### RibbonShape.activity

The indicator and list of the RunningActivityScope sit in the left container, just right of the collapse chevron. While nothing is running, the spinner isn't there, and the left container shrinks around the project indicator and the chevron.

### RibbonShape.projectIndicator

The ProjectIndicator leads the left container, a solid block the full height of the bar down to the line along its bottom, ending on that line. It is the same height, and what it shows is in the same place, whether the ribbon is expanded or collapsed. There is no divider between it and what

### RibbonShape.groups

Each group has its title in muted text rotated -90deg (bottom to top) aligned along the left edge of the group naming what its commands have in common. The title sits on a strip with a slightly different background colour, at 12px, with generous padding either side of it within the strip, which runs the full height of the commands' area, with no padding above or below it, 8 pixels from the buttons beside it. The first group's strip sits flush against the left edge of the commands' area, with no space before it. Groups sit side by side, 8 pixels apart, with no divider between them: each group's title strip is what marks where it starts.
A tab with no commands reads "No commands yet".

### RibbonShape.commands

A command button is one of two sizes, and each tab says which of its commands are which:

- full: its large icon above its label, exactly two slim buttons stacked tall
- slim: 22 pixels tall, its small icon to the left of its label
- small: only in the collapsed ribbon: 22 pixels tall, its small icon to the left of its label, and only as wide as they are

Buttons side by side are 8 pixels apart. Slim buttons side by side stack down instead, top aligned, two to a column, each column as wide as its widest button and each button as wide as its column; a third starts the next column, 8 pixels along. A full button always stands alone. A slim button fills only its column's width: nowhere does a button stretch to fill a row.
Every command starts from the top of its group, so the commands of a tab all start at the same line. A full button is always two slim buttons stacked tall, never shorter or taller, however much its icon and label would take, alone or beside any column.
Every button is square, with no rounded corners. Its background is clearly apart from the commands' area behind it, though still quiet: white laid a seventh of the way over that area in dark mode, and not quite half way in light mode, rather than a colour of its own, so it stays as far apart from a tinted body too, lighter in both modes, and more so while hovered; while pressed it darkens instead. An on or off setting, like dark mode, is a switch rather than a button, sitting in a block with a button's colour, as wide as a button of its size and as tall as the switch and its label need.
A command's tooltip explains what it does rather than repeating its label, and gives its keyboard shortcut if it has one.
A command can be marked primary; each tab says which of its commands are.
A command that can't run is disabled, not hidden, and its tooltip says why.

### RibbonShape.height

The commands drive the height: the command area is as tall as the tallest column of the open tabs, padded 8 pixels above and below, and nothing more. Since no column holds more than two slim buttons, and a full button is two slim buttons tall, the tallest the command area gets is two slim buttons with 8 pixels between them, padded: 68 pixels, and never more. A tab whose tallest column is two slim buttons, or that has a full button, is taller than one of a single slim button, and a tab with no commands, which is only its "No commands yet" padded the same way, is the shortest of all. So switching tabs can change the command area's height, and the window beneath moves with it.
Every group is as tall as the command area, so the groups' title strips run its full height whichever tab is open.
There are 8 pixels of padding at the right end but none at the left: the first group's title strip starts right at the command area's left edge. "No commands yet" keeps 8 pixels from that edge. The groups' title strips are not padded, and run the command area's full height, with each title centred down its strip whatever that height is.

### RibbonShape.collapsing

The ribbon collapses, and expands again, with a chevron button in the left container, after the project indicator, by double-clicking a tab, or with Ctrl+F1 (Cmd+F1 on macOS). Whether it is collapsed is one of the UserPreferencesScope.
The chevron button is square, 22 pixels on each side, its icon centred in it. It is the same size, and its icon the same size, whether the ribbon is expanded or collapsed: only the way the chevron points changes.
Collapsed, the tabs go away too. The ribbon becomes a single thin row, exactly as tall as the row of tabs is when expanded, its bottom line where the tab row's is, so collapsing or expanding moves nothing above that line, led by the left container, the same as beside the tabs, the project indicator filling the row's height, and then every primary command, from all of the tabs, as small buttons: a small icon beside its label, and dark mode as a small switch in a block only as wide as the switch and its label. Every one is only as wide as its own icon and label, 8 pixels from the next, whatever the tab it comes from calls it; a command that is slim in its tab doesn't grow to fill the row. They keep the order of their tabs, with a thin vertical divider between the commands of one tab and the next, and keep their tooltips and disabled states. The right container, when it holds anything, ends the row. Every control in the row, the dividers and the containers' contents included, is vertically centred in it.
When the commands and dividers are wider than the room between the left container and the right container, or the right end of the row, that stretch of the row scrolls sideways, as the expanded command area does. The containers stay where they are, never scrolled away or squeezed, and nothing in the row shrinks to fit.

## ThemeShape

Anchor in `spec/ui/theme/index.pi`, declared as a `shape`, extending `Shape`.

### ThemeShape.description

Type: `string`. Overrides `Shape.description`.

The theme is defined by its dark mode, built around a base grey of #444444. Dark mode is the reference: every colour below is chosen for it first, and light mode is its reasonable interpretation on a light base, keeping the same roles, the same order, and steps of about the same size. The greys are true neutrals, with no hint of blue or warmth. There are no gradients, and no texture. Everything that uses a colour names its role here rather than a value of its own, so the two modes stay coherent.

### ThemeShape.hierarchy

How far a colour is from the base, in contrast, says how much it stands out, and that holds everywhere. The base is the quiet ground of the window. A step away is structure: panels, controls, and the lines between them. Further away is what is worked on: text, content, and the wells that hold it. Furthest away is state and meaning: what is selected, focused, or needs attention. Nothing structural is ever further from the base than the content it frames, and nothing decorative is ever as far as state. A hover is always a smaller step than a selection, and a selection a smaller step than focus.

### ThemeShape.surfaces

Each surface in dark mode, then light mode:

- well, #2e2e2e, then #f5f5f5: where content is read or written, such as the editor, code blocks, answers, and task tables' bodies; the most contrast with the text it holds
- recessed, #383838, then #e8e8e8: text inputs, lists, and trees, a step toward the well
- base, #444444, then #d0d0d0: the window, its panels, the sidebar, and the ribbon's command area
- raised, #4e4e4e, then #dadada: buttons, tab bars, headers, a group's title strip, and cards, a small step toward the viewer
- hover, #585858, then #e2e2e2: a raised or listed thing under the pointer, one step further along the way it is already raised
- pressed, #3c3c3c, then #c6c6c6: a control held down, a step back past the base
- selected, #5e5e5e, then #bcbcbc: a selected row or tab without focus, the neutral state furthest from its surface short of the accent
- overlay, #4a4a4a, then #dcdcdc: floating surfaces, such as menus, popovers, tooltips, the completion menu, and inset panels

### ThemeShape.lightMode

Light mode reads the dark ladder on a light base of #d0d0d0. Wells and inputs go lighter, toward white, so they keep the most contrast with the dark text they hold, just as they are darker in dark mode for the same reason. Raised controls and floating surfaces go a smaller step lighter too, so they still come forward, and hover goes further the same way. Pressed and selected go darker, and so do lines. Text is dark on light.

### ThemeShape.text

Text in dark mode, then light mode:

- primary, #ebebeb, then #1e1e1e: the foreground, for anything read
- secondary, #c4c4c4, then #454545: what the spec calls muted, such as paths, counts, and descriptions
- tertiary, #9c9c9c, then #636363: dimmer than muted, such as help text and placeholders
- disabled, #7a7a7a, then #8c8c8c: what can't be used now

### ThemeShape.lines

Lines are one pixel, and quieter than anything they separate:

- line, #3a3a3a, then #bdbdbd: dividers between areas, table rows, and list rows
- edge, #2a2a2a, then #a6a6a6: the border of controls, inputs, and floating surfaces, darker than the base in both modes, what the spec calls the border colour

A line is never doubled. Wherever two things that each have a border meet, a single line is drawn between them, never two side by side: one of them leaves that side out, or the two overlap so their lines lie on the same pixels. A thing that fills what holds it leaves out the sides the holder already draws, and a row in a stack draws only the line between it and the row before. This holds while things move too, such as a row sliding into a stack, apart from a frame or two. A focus ring, or an accent bar marking what is current, isn't a border in this sense, and may sit against one. A gpui-kit component used with its default styling, such as tabs in a tab bar, keeps its own borders as gpui-kit draws them; only its colours are the theme's.

### ThemeShape.accent

One accent, a calm blue, is the only colour that means selection, focus, or the primary action:

- accent, #7fb4ea, then #1f5fa6: focus rings, the underline of a selected tab, links, a selection's edge, and accent text
- accent fill, #3d6a98, then #2b68ad: primary buttons, with primary text in white in both modes, and a selected item in a focused list
- selection, the accent fill at 35% over its surface: selected text

What the spec calls the theme's primary colour, or its focus ring colour, is the accent.

### ThemeShape.status

Status colours are kept for what they mean, readable as text on the base and every surface darker than it in dark mode, and on the base and every surface lighter than it in light mode:

- success, #8fd095, then #2c6e31: done, added, aligned
- warning, #e6bb68, then #8a5a00: running out, modified, drifting
- error, #f0928a, then #b3261e: failed, removed, diverged
- information, the accent: running, informational notes

Two more hues, for telling kinds of things apart rather than for status:

- purple, #bba0e6, then #6b4aa6
- cyan, #78c8ce, then #1f6f78

Wherever the spec names a hue for what is shown, it means the theme's: blue is the accent, green success, amber or yellow warning, red error, purple and cyan the hues above, and grey tertiary text.
A tint of a colour, such as a prompt mode's or a changed line's, is that colour laid over its surface at low strength, never enough to take the text on it below its contrast.

### ThemeShape.bevel

A surface that should lift slightly off what it sits on, such as a scrollbar's thumb or a table's header, can have the theme's bevel: a very slight 1 pixel edge around it, just enough to lift it. Its top and left edges are a touch lighter, as white laid faintly over the surface, 8% in dark mode and 55% in light mode; its bottom and right edges only barely darker, as black laid very faintly over it, 6% in dark mode and 3% in light mode, far subtler than the light and never reading as a line. Laid over rather than a colour of its own, it looks the same on any surface, hovered, pressed, or tinted. The lit top runs the full width, and the lit left side runs beneath it; the shaded bottom runs the full width, and the shaded right side runs above it, so no two edges overlap. It sits inside the surface, taking no room, and isn't a border in the sense of lines never being doubled.
A surface being pressed in can have the bevel pressed instead: the same edges, with the light and shade swapped, so its top and left edges are barely darker and its bottom and right edges a touch lighter.

### ThemeShape.elevation

Floating surfaces sit on the overlay surface with an edge border, and are the only things with a shadow: soft, short, and black, stronger in dark mode than in light. Behind a modal surface, such as an inset panel, the window is dimmed with black, 40% in dark mode and 25% in light mode.

### ThemeShape.contrast

However the colours are used, primary and secondary text keep at least 4.5 to 1 against the base, recessed, well, and overlay surfaces, and primary text at least 4 to 1 on controls in any state. Tertiary text, status colours, and the accent keep at least 3 to 1 on the base. Edges keep about 1.5 to 1 against the base, and lines less.

### ThemeShape.gpuiKit

The application's gpui-kit theme is set from these roles in both modes, so a component with gpui-kit's default styling follows the theme with nothing of its own: its background is the base, its foreground primary text, its muted foreground secondary text, its border the edge, its input and list backgrounds recessed, its popover the overlay, its primary and ring the accent, and its success, warning, and danger the status colours.

### ThemeShape.modes

Which mode shows is up to the application: see the MainWindowScope.

## RunningActivityShape

Anchor in `spec/scope/running-activity/index.pi`, declared as a `shape`, extending `Shape`.

### RunningActivityShape.description

Type: `string`. Overrides `Shape.description`.

What counts as work still running in the application, and how each is listed, newest last.

### RunningActivityShape.running

- the task the harness is working on, from the PromptEditor, headed "Task" with the first line of its prompt
- each question still running, from the ChatInputScope's Ask tab, headed "Question" with its first line
- a spec build run on its own, as the SpecBuildScope says, "Building the spec"
- a divergence analysis in the DivergenceScope, "Analyzing divergence"
- a search for concepts to rescope in the RescopeScope, "Finding scopes to extract"

Prompts waiting in the queue don't count as running, since they are saved with the project, and neither does a panel whose work is over.
Tasks, questions, and spec builds count in every open project of the OpenProjectsScope, not only the one on screen. Those of the project on screen come first, then each other project's, its rows headed with that project's folder name after the kind, such as "Task · my-project".

### RunningActivityShape.indicator

While anything is running, a small spinner shows, with how many things are running beside it when more than one is. Its tooltip says what is running, or how many things are. While nothing is, neither shows, and nothing takes their place. Where it sits is up to what holds it.

### RunningActivityShape.list

Clicking the spinner opens a small list beneath it of everything running, one row each, in the order above, each with a small spinner of its own. Clicking a row closes the list and reveals what it is, first switching to its project when it belongs to another:

- a task brings back the latest task's output, closing the previous tasks and any inset panel over it, and scrolls it to the end
- a question closes the answer drawer and any inset panel, so its row is in view
- a divergence analysis or a rescope search brings its MinimizablePanelScope back
- a spec build has nothing to show, so its row only closes the list

Pressing the mouse outside the list, or <Escape>, closes it too, as does everything in it finishing.

### RunningActivityShape.quitting

Quitting, however it is asked for, while the harness is working on a task or a question, or while a spec build runs on its own, in any open project, asks first. A divergence analysis or a rescope search doesn't ask, and quitting stops it. The message is titled "Quit while a task is running?" and says what is still running: the harness working on a prompt, piton build, or both, and, when it runs in more than one project, in how many projects. "Quit" exits, and "Keep Running" or <Escape> dismisses it. Asking to quit again while it is open doesn't open a second one, and an open palette closes first.

## ProjectIndicatorShape

Anchor in `spec/ui/components/project-indicator/index.pi`, declared as a `shape`, extending `Shape`.

### ProjectIndicatorShape.description

Type: `string`. Overrides `Shape.description`.

A solid block, the full height of wherever it sits, in its own colour: pure black in dark mode, darker than every surface around it, and a text input's background, the theme's well surface, in light mode. It has no border and no rounded corners. In it, a small folder icon, then the name of the project open through the ProjectDirectoryScope, which is its folder's name, in medium weight, vertically centred. The whole block is what is clicked, filling it edge to edge, square, and it highlights on hover.

### ProjectIndicatorShape.noProject

While no project is open, as the NoProjectStateScope says, it reads "No project", muted, after the same icon, and has no tooltip.

### ProjectIndicatorShape.tooltip

While a project is open, its tooltip gives the project's full path.

### ProjectIndicatorShape.recentProjects

Clicking it, or pressing <Ctrl+`> (<Cmd+`> on macOS) anywhere in the window, opens a list of the recent projects of the ProjectDirectoryScope, up to five, newest first; doing so again closes it. Like the palette, the shortcut does nothing while an inset panel is open.
The list hangs flush from the indicator: its top edge is the indicator's bottom edge and its left edge the indicator's, at least 360 pixels wide. It is a solid block in the indicator's own colour, with no rounded corners, and a thin edge along its sides and bottom but none along its top, where it meets the indicator. While it is open, the rest of the window is dimmed as behind an inset panel, and the indicator stays undimmed above the dimming, so the two read as one.
At the top of the list, a filter field with a search icon takes the keyboard as the list opens. Typing filters the projects fuzzily, as the palette matches, by folder name or full path, the best matches first; with nothing typed, all of them show, newest first. <Up> and <Down> move a highlight through the rows, wrapping around, starting on the first row whenever the filter changes, and <Enter> picks the highlighted row.
Each project is a row with its folder name in medium weight above its full path, muted, after a folder icon, or a tick for the project open now. A busy project, of the OpenProjectsScope, shows a small spinner at the right end of its row, and beneath its path, muted, what is running in it, such as "Task running", "2 questions running", or "Building the spec", joined with a middle dot. A busy project is listed even when it is no longer among the five most recent, after them. Rows reach the list's edges, with no rounded corners, and highlight on hover. Picking a row, by clicking or <Enter>, closes the list and switches to that project, or just closes it for the one already open. Switching never stops what is running in the project switched from. Once switched, the chat input takes the keyboard, ready to write to the project switched to. Clicking the indicator, clicking the dimmed window, or <Escape> closes it.
The last row, beneath a thin divider, whatever the filter leaves, reads "Open Project…" after a folder icon, and closes the list and opens the OpenProjectScope.

### ProjectIndicatorShape.width

A name wider than 320 pixels is cut off with an ellipsis.

### ProjectIndicatorShape.following

It always shows the project open now: opening, creating, or switching to another project changes it straight away.

### ProjectIndicatorShape.busyElsewhere

While another open project is busy, a small dot in the accent colour sits after the name, and the tooltip adds how many other projects are busy.

#### Ribbon

### MainWindowShape.body

#### Sidebar

ProjectSidebarScope

#### Open File

A file opened, from the FileTreeScope or anywhere else the OpenFileScope says, shows in an EditorScope, in a split beside the chat history: the file on the left taking 50% of the width, the chat history on the right taking the rest. The split can be resized by dragging its edge. Closing the file closes the split.
When the split opens, it slides in from the sidebar, so it's clear where it came from: the file's side grows out of the sidebar's edge to its share of the width, the file sliding into view from behind that edge as it does, over the chat history. The chat history keeps its width while the file slides over it, so nothing in it is laid out anew each frame, and takes the rest of the width once the slide settles.
The slide is quick and settles without bouncing, and only then can the split be dragged. A file opened in place of one already showing doesn't slide, since the split is already open. The ChatInputScope is never split: it stays along the bottom, across the full width of prompt mode.
Closing the file plays the slide in reverse, back into the

##### Sidebar

the file's side shrinks from whatever width it was

dragged to down to nothing at the sidebar's edge, the file sliding out of view behind that edge as it does, uncovering the chat history, which is back across the full width beneath it from the start of the slide. It is as quick as the slide in, and settles without bouncing. Opening a file while one is still sliding out slides the new one in straight away.

#### Open Diff

A file's DiffViewScope, opened from the FileTreeScope, opens in an InsetPanelScope. It leaves the split alone: any file open there stays open, unsaved changes and all. Opening another file's diff replaces the one in the panel, as does opening one while a new project is being set up. Opening the file from the diff closes the panel and opens the file, as the OpenFileScope says.

#### Analyze Divergence

The ribbon's Analyze Divergence command opens the DivergenceScope as a MinimizablePanelScope, to analyze, in place of whatever else is open there, or brings back one that was minimized.

#### Rescope

The ribbon's Rescope command opens the RescopeScope as a MinimizablePanelScope, in place of whatever else is open there, or brings back one that was minimized. Its Refactor sends its prompt to the prompt mode on the application's behalf, as the PromptSendingScope says.

#### View Divergence Reports

The ribbon's View Divergence Reports command opens the DivergenceScope the same way, to view the reports, without starting an analysis.

#### New Project

The ribbon's New Project command opens the NewProjectScope in an InsetPanelScope, fresh each time, in place of any diff open there. Once the project is created, the panel closes and the new project is open.

#### Open Project

The Open Project commands, from the ribbon or the palette, show the OpenProjectScope in an InsetPanelScope, in place of whatever else is open there.

#### Settings

The settings, opened with Ctrl+, (Cmd+, on macOS), the ribbon's Settings command, or the palette, show the SettingsWindowScope in an InsetPanelScope, in place of whatever else is open there.

#### Prompt Mode

The body displays the PromptEditor and any splits, to the right of the ProjectSidebarScope.

## PaletteShape

Anchor in `spec/scope/palette/index.pi`, declared as a `shape`, extending `Shape`.

### PaletteShape.description

Type: `string`. Overrides `Shape.description`.

A popover near the top of the window, over a dimmed backdrop: a tab bar using gpui-kit's default tab styling, a search field beneath it, and the results beneath that.

### PaletteShape.opening

Ctrl+P (Cmd+P on macOS) anywhere in the window opens the palette on the Files tab with an empty search and focus in the search field. Pressing it again while the palette is open closes it.

### PaletteShape.closing

Picking a result closes the palette. Esc clears the search, and closes the palette once the search is empty. Clicking outside the palette closes it. Closing it without picking anything puts focus back where it was.

### PaletteShape.tabs

```
overview: The tabs are Files, System, Commands, Skills, and Agents, in that order. Each lists its own results. The search is kept when switching tabs, and applies to the tab switched to.
switching: Clicking a tab switches to it. <Tab> moves to the next tab and <Shift+Tab> to the previous one, wrapping around, and focus stays in the search field.
files: Every file in the selected ProjectDirectoryScope, listed as the ProjectLocationsScope lists the files under a folder. Picking a file opens it, as the OpenFileScope says. Until a project is picked the tab reads "No project open", as the NoProjectStateScope says.
fileSearch: On the Files tab, Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on macOS) sends the search to a separate harness run that finds the file being described, even when files match. Plain Enter does the same once the file list has loaded and nothing matches; otherwise it picks the highlighted file. While nothing matches, the results area says so and how to search with the harness instead, reading "No results. Press Enter to perform an agentic search." in place of "No matches". While the search runs, the results area shows its TaskTableScope, scrolling with a ScrollbarScope with no lock to the bottom. When it finishes, a single file closes the palette and opens that file, several files show a "Multiple results were found" alert, and no files adds a "No file matching the search was found." row. Changing the search or switching tabs stops the run and brings back the normal results, and if the palette closes while it runs, nothing opens.
fileSearchSystemPrompt: The search's system prompt, file-search.pi, of the BakedSystemPromptsScope, is appended to the harness's own. It tells the harness we're really trying to find the one file being asked for, giving several only when they are all equally what was asked for; to only read and never change anything; and to stop as soon as it is confident. It lists where to look, in this order of priority, preferring a match from an earlier place over an equally good match from a later one: the spec location; the code location; `.suspense`; then `.claude`, the locations being those of the ProjectLocationsScope. The harness's final reply is only JSON listing the files by path relative to the project, and paths that don't exist are dropped.
system: The application's own commands, each doing what its toolbar control or shortcut does: "Open Project…", which opens the OpenProjectScope, "Build", "Dark mode" or "Light mode" (whichever is not the current one), "Settings…", which opens the SettingsWindowScope, and "Quit". Build builds the spec on its own, as the SpecBuildScope says.
commands: The commands of the HarnessCatalogScope.
skills: The skills of the HarnessCatalogScope.
agents: The agents of the HarnessCatalogScope.
mentions: A command, skill, or agent shows its description when it has one. Picking one inserts it into the ChatInputScope at the cursor as a mention, as the HarnessCatalogScope says, with a space before it when the cursor follows other text. Focus then moves to the chat input.
```

### PaletteShape.fuzzySearch

A result matches when the search's characters all appear in it in order, ignoring case, though not necessarily next to each other. The best matches come first: runs of consecutive characters, and characters at the start of a word or of a file's name, rank higher, then shorter results. The matched characters are highlighted. With an empty search, files are listed by path, the application's commands in the order above, and the harness's by name. At most the 100 best results are listed.

### PaletteShape.keyboard

Up and Down move the highlight, which starts on the first result, and Enter picks the highlighted result. Clicking a result picks it.

### ChatInputShape.hiddenAnchor

While the user will be able to type plain text, behind the scenes, they'll be typing into a randomly-named piton anchor with a userPrompt property.  It's this compiled anchor that will be send to the HarnessIntegrationScope

#### Escaping

A prompt may hold anything, text pasted into it included, so it isn't written into the anchor as Piton prose, where braces, colons, leading dashes, code fences, comments, indentation, and backslashes all mean something. The anchor is exported, so that it compiles, and its userPrompt is a multi-line escape block, which Piton keeps exactly as it is: the prompt's lines, each at the block's indentation, fenced by a line of three backslashes, or of one more than any line of the prompt made only of backslashes, so nothing in it closes the block early. The systemPrompt is written the same way.
Each at-brace or dollar-brace around a dotted path of identifiers whose first name is imported, in the userPrompt and then the systemPrompt, is also listed once, in the order they first appear, as an item of the anchor's references property, left out when there are none; a reference to a name that isn't imported, such as a pasted shell variable, is only text. `piton compile` resolves the references. What the harness receives is the prompt as it was saved, line for line, with each reference replaced by what it resolved to: a dollar-brace by its text, and an at-brace by a Markdown link, from the project directory, to the reference document the project's build writes for it, in the reference root of the config's first adapter, such as .claude/reference, named by its dotted path, and going to the heading for the anchor or property it names once the document is built. A prompt saved by an earlier version, as quoted pieces or as prose, still reads back.

#### Auto Imports

The names a prompt uses are imported however the prompt got there, typed, completed, or pasted. What `piton lsp` is shown while the prompt is typed is the prompt as prose, line for line and position for position as typed, but with anything outside a reference other than letters, digits, and spaces between words blanked out, character for character. Pasted text with an unclosed quote or brace, a code fence, deeper indentation, or what would be a comment then never stops the server finding the names that need importing, both as completions are offered and when the prompt is sent.

#### Attached Text

A prompt with attached text gives the hidden anchor an attachedText

##### Property

a list with an item per attached piece of text, in the

order they were attached, keyed text1, text2, and so on. Since attached text is taken as it is, not as Piton, each is written as a multi-line escape block, as the userPrompt is, so nothing in it is interpolated or evaluated. A prompt with nothing attached has no attachedText property.
What the harness receives is the compiled userPrompt followed by the attached text: a line reading "Attached text:", then each piece as a fenced code block, whose fence is longer than any run of backticks in the text itself. This is also the compiled prompt shown in the task's header.

#### Sliced

A prompt sent with Slice on is still written as the hidden anchor, which records that it was sliced, and is compiled the same way, so a prompt that fails to compile fails with Slice on too. But what the harness receives is the prompt as it was saved, line for line, with each at-brace reference replaced by the dotted path it names rather than a link, and each dollar-brace by its text, as ever. Then, for each at-brace reference in the userPrompt, once, in the order they first appear, what `piton slice` prints for it, run in the project directory on the source file and dotted path the reference names, under a line reading "Spec slices:". A slice that fails puts why in its place, and the prompt is still sent. Attached text follows the slices, as it follows the prompt. The system prompt is resolved as ever. A queued prompt keeps whether it was sliced, and the preview shows what the harness would receive with the toggle as it is.

### DivergenceShape.results

#### Connections

A connection joins a source file and a spec file. Its strength is the average of what both agents said of it, or what one said when only one mentioned it, from 0 to 1, and so is its divergence, which is unknown when neither agent said. Connections to files that aren't among the source or spec files are left out.

#### Measures

Each file analyzed has:

- its influence: how strongly it is connected to the other side, 1 less the product of 1 less each connection's strength, so one strong connection or several weaker ones both count for a lot, and a file with no connections has none
- its divergence: what its agent said
- its definition: how well defined its agent said it is, with the gaps in the spec or the blanks the implementation filled in

A file its agent left out is "Not analyzed", and counts towards none of the figures below. Each is shown as a whole percentage.

#### Score

The divergence score is the average divergence of every file analyzed, source and spec alike, and the alignment is 100% less it. The header reads as the alignment, after a thin divider beside the panel's title, a little larger and bolder than the title: for a divergence score of 8%, "92% aligned". It is coloured by what the score means, in the ThemeScope's status colours: green while the score is below 20%, aligned; amber from 20% up to 50%, drifting; and red from 50%, diverged. Beside it, muted, how long ago the report was made. The header is the same height whether the analysis is running or its results are shown.

#### Tabs

Beneath the header, a row of tabs, "Report", "Source", and "Spec", each its label alone: muted, brightening on hover, and while selected, in the foreground colour and underlined in the theme's primary colour, the underline sitting on the row's bottom border. The labels line up with the content beneath. Once an analysis is over, or a saved report is opened, "Report" is showing.

#### Report

The Report tab is an overall assessment, scrolling with a ScrollbarScope. Its sections are headed a little larger than its text, and their parts by small, muted labels; everything lines up along its left edge, and from the assessment on, it is laid out in two columns of equal width, top aligned:

- a row of figures, each a bordered card with its value large above what it is: the alignment, coloured as the header's; the definition of the source files and of the spec files, each the average of their files', coloured green when well defined, amber, or red as the score would be for how poorly defined they are; the coverage of each side, the share of its analyzed files with at least one connection; and how many files are aligned, drifting, and diverged, by their divergence's percentage
- "Assessment": the code's on the left and the spec's on the right, each under its side's name, as the agents wrote them
- "Well defined" on the left and "Less well defined" on the right: the areas the agents named, each its name and why, muted
- beneath them, starting level with each other, the five best defined files on the left, highest first, and the five least well defined on the right, lowest first, each with its definition
- "Most diverged" on the left: the five files that diverge most, source and spec alike; and "Saved reports" on the right: each report saved for the project, newest first, with how long ago it was made and how aligned it was, the one showing marked; clicking another shows it
- "Notes", when there are any notes about the analysis

Hovering a figure, or the header's alignment, shows a tooltip, as described under tooltips, explaining what it means:

- Aligned: how closely the code and the spec agree, 100% less the average divergence of every file analyzed, source and spec alike, green above 80%, amber above 50%, and red otherwise
- Source definition: how much of the code the spec defines, averaged over the source files, low meaning the implementation filled in a lot the spec never says
- Spec definition: how precisely the spec describes what to build, averaged over the spec files, low meaning gaps an implementation has to guess at
- Source coverage: the share of source files connected to at least one spec file, a source file with no connection not being driven by the spec at all
- Spec coverage: the share of spec files at least one source file implements, a spec file with no connection not being built, or not traceable to the code
- Aligned, drifting, and diverged: how many files analyzed are aligned, diverging less than 20%; drifting, from 20% up to 50%; and diverged, 50% or more

A file in any of these lists is a row of its path and its percentage at the column's right, and opens that file in its tree when clicked. Rows highlight on hover, and the highlight reaches a little past the text, which stays in line with the headings.

#### Trees

"Source" and "Spec" show that side's files as a tree: a row per folder and file, indented by depth, folders before files, each sorted by name. A file's row shows its name, a small bar, and a percentage. In the Source tree, they are the file's divergence, coloured as the score is; in the Spec tree, the file's definition, coloured green when well defined, amber, or red, as the report's definition figures are. A file its agent left out reads "Not analyzed" in their place, and a spec file whose definition its agent didn't give, as in reports made before definition was measured, reads "No definition". The tree scrolls with a ScrollbarScope.
Clicking a file selects it, and beside the tree, the selected file's details show, as in a RankedSelectionListScope, though the tree has no checkboxes or action. The details are its path and summary, then its measures, each with a bar:

- influence, as "Influence"
- divergence, for a source file as "Diverges from the spec", and for a spec file as "Implementation diverges", coloured as the score is
- definition, as "Definition"

Then, for a source file, "Filled in by the implementation", and for a spec file, "Gaps in the spec", listing them, or saying there are none. Then its connections to files on the other side, strongest first, each with the other file's path, a bar as long as the connection is strong, its strength as a percentage, labelled by which way the influence runs: for a source file, "Influence from spec", and for a spec file, "Influence on code"; its divergence as a percentage when known, coloured as the score is, and what the agents noted of it. Clicking a connection switches to the other tree with that file selected and scrolled into view. With nothing selected, the details say to select a file. Once the results are in, the source file with the highest divergence is selected.

Each analysis that gets results, even with one agent failed, is saved as soon as it is over as a report among the project's data, as the ProjectDataScope says, with everything the report shows: its files and their measures, the connections, the assessments and areas, and its notes. ### DivergenceShape.tooltips

Everything in the panel that stands for something explains itself with a tooltip when hovered a moment: what it's called, then, muted and wrapped to a readable width, what it represents. Besides the report's figures and the header's alignment:

- the header's age: when the analysis behind the report finished and it was saved, kept with the project so it survives a restart
- "Analyze again": that it runs a fresh analysis, the report shown staying among the saved reports
- each tab: Report, an overall assessment of the project; Source, every source file with how far it diverges from the spec; Spec, every spec file with how well defined it is; each tree's saying a file can be selected for its measures and connections
- a tree row's bar and percentage: a source file's divergence, from doing just what the spec describes to nothing in the spec accounting for it; a spec file's definition, from too vague to build from to leaving nothing to guess
- "Not analyzed": that its agent left the file out, so it has no measures and counts towards no figure; "No definition", that its agent didn't say how well defined the file is
- each measure in a file's details: its influence, how strongly it's connected to the other side, one strong connection or several weaker ones both counting for a lot; its divergence and definition, as for the trees, from its own side
- the gaps' title: for a source file, what the implementation decided that the spec never says; for a spec file, what it leaves out or vague, so an implementation has to guess
- a connection's influence: how much the spec file drove the source file, or the source file is built from the spec file, from barely any to written straight from it; and its divergence, how far the source file diverges from that spec file in particular
- the report's headings: the assessment, what each agent made of its side; the well and less well defined areas, each with why; the best and least well defined files, and those that diverge most, source and spec alike, each opening in its tree when clicked; and the saved reports, newest first, each shown when clicked

## GitPanelShape

Anchor in `spec/ui/components/git-panel/index.pi`, declared as a `shape`, extending `Shape`.

### GitPanelShape.description

Type: `string`. Overrides `Shape.description`.

A compact panel. It is shown only while the project is inside a git repository.

### GitPanelShape.branch

The top row shows the branch from the GitScope, or "Detached HEAD", beside how many commits it is ahead of its upstream (↑) and behind it (↓), each only when not zero. At the right end are a Pull button and a Push button, icons with tooltips.

### GitPanelShape.summary

Below the branch, a line counts the GitScope's changes, leaving out any kind with none, as "2 modified · 1 untracked", or "No changes". Beside it, how many lines were added (+, in green) and removed (−, in red). The files themselves are not listed, since the FileTreeScope shows them. The summary refreshes as the GitScope does, and straight after anything the panel does.

### GitPanelShape.commitNotes

Above the message box, a row for each commit note, in the order they were added: a one-line box holding the note, which can be edited, and a small button to remove it. Each task that adds a note, as the PromptModesScope says, adds a one-line summary of what it changed, once the harness has written it, quickly, in the same way as a written

#### Message

from what the task asked and the harness's own summary of what

it did, at most 72 characters in the imperative mood, as commit-note.pi, of the BakedSystemPromptsScope, asks. Notes are saved with the project's data, as the ProjectDataScope says, as they are added, edited, and removed, so they survive a restart, and are never themselves committed.

### GitPanelShape.message

A commit message box, a GrowingTextInputScope growing to 10 rows at most, so it starts at a single row. It reads "Commit message" while empty.

### GitPanelShape.writingAMessage

A "Write message" button, with a sparkles icon, has the harness write the commit message from what has changed, and puts it in the message box, replacing what was there. It is quick: a small, fast model, at low effort, with no tools, handed only the list of changed files and as much of the diff as fits in a small, fixed amount. The message is a summary line of at most 72 characters in the imperative mood, followed, only if it helps, by a few short bullet points, as commit-message.pi, of the BakedSystemPromptsScope, asks. The button is disabled while there are no changes.

### GitPanelShape.committing

A primary "Commit" button commits every change, new files included. The commit message is what was typed, then a blank line, then each note that isn't blank as a line of its own starting "- "; with nothing typed, it is the notes alone. Once committed, the message box and the notes are cleared. It is disabled while there is neither a message nor a note, or there are no changes.

### GitPanelShape.pushingAndPulling

Push pushes the branch, setting its upstream on origin first if it has none.
Pull fetches the branch's upstream. With nothing new it says the branch is already up to date. When only the upstream has moved on, the branch fast-forwards to it. When both have moved on, the upstream is merged in automatically, as long as the merge has no conflicts. If it would conflict, the pull is cancelled before anything changes: the branch, its files, and the index stay exactly as they were, no merge is left in progress, and an error names the files that would have conflicted. Pull is disabled while the branch has no upstream.

### GitPanelShape.feedback

While the panel is committing, pushing, pulling, or writing a message, that button shows a spinner and the others are disabled. Committing, pushing, and pulling say so in a notification when they succeed; a pull says whether it was already up to date, pulled, or pulled and merged. Anything that fails says why in an error notification.

## ScrollbarShape

Anchor in `spec/ui/components/scrollbar/index.pi`, declared as a `shape`, extending `Shape`.

### ScrollbarShape.description

Type: `string`. Overrides `Shape.description`.

A narrow column along the right of the list, always shown, whether or not the list has anything to scroll. It is the list's only scrollbar: no scrollbar is laid over the list, or appears only while hovering or scrolling.

### ScrollbarShape.buttons

A square button at the top of the column scrolls the list up a little, and a square button at the bottom scrolls it down a little. The column is as wide as the buttons, with the track's line, are tall. Each button sits just inside the track, as the thumb does, never over the track's

#### Edges

the track's line runs down the column's side against the list

beside it too, unbroken from the top of the column to the bottom, the button filling the width inside that line, and a pixel of the dark track lies between the button and the rest of the track, and between the down button and the lock button. The buttons draw no lines of their own; whatever holds the column draws the lines around it. The buttons have no background of their own: they are the colour of whatever the column sits on, until hovered or pressed. While the pointer is over the up or down button, it has the bevel of the ThemeScope, and while it is pressed with the pointer still over it, its pressed bevel instead; neither bevel shows otherwise, and neither takes the mouse.

### ScrollbarShape.track

Between the buttons, a track holds a thumb as tall as the share of the list in view, and never too short to grab, placed as far down the track as the list is scrolled. The thumb is a plain rectangle with no rounded corners, filling the track inside the track's own line, never covering it, so the line beside the list runs unbroken the track's full height, beside the thumb too. It has the bevel of the ThemeScope, whether or not it is hovered or dragged. The track is dark: black laid over whatever the column sits on, rather than a colour of its own, so it is clearly darker than that surface, in both modes, and looks the same on any surface. Beyond its bevel, the thumb has no border or line of its own, and no background of its own: it is the colour of whatever the column sits on, the same as the buttons, so it reads as a gap of the surface in the dark track. It lightens a step while the pointer is over it, as white laid over it, and another step while it is being dragged, and goes back as soon as neither is true. The track has a thin line down its side against the list, in the theme's border colour, the column's full height, beside the buttons as well as the thumb. With nothing to scroll, the thumb fills the track. Pressing the thumb and dragging scrolls the list with it for as long as the button is held, even once the pointer leaves the column, and pressing the track elsewhere moves the thumb there, from where it can be dragged straight away.

### ScrollbarShape.steadiness

The thumb never jumps. Its size and place always reflect the whole list's real height, including a list that only draws the rows in view: every row is measured, even those never scrolled into view, so the thumb doesn't grow, shrink, or leap as rows come into view. A row that arrives, or changes, while out of view counts at its height as soon as it does, and after the list's width changes, rewrapping its rows, the height is known in full again by the next frame. Only what has changed is measured again, so a long list stays as quick to scroll and to add to as one that measures only what is in view; only a change of width measures every row again.
A row's height is the same measured out of view as drawn in it. Text in a row, such as a reply's markdown, is parsed once and kept for as long as the app runs, not only while its row is drawn, so a row scrolled away and back is never parsed again, nor shorter for a moment while it is. Long text is parsed in the background, so a row holding it may first measure short: while it parses, its row is measured again every fraction of a second, for a few seconds at most, so the height is right as soon as the parse lands, whether or not the row is in view. Dragging the thumb, it stays under the pointer the whole way, rows coming into view or not.

### ScrollbarShape.lockToBottom

A list that keeps receiving output, like a task's, adds one more square button below the others that locks the scroll to the bottom. While it is locked, the button shows as selected and the list stays scrolled to the bottom as output arrives. Pressing it again unlocks it. Its tooltip says which it will do.

#### Lock Pulse

Whenever the scroll becomes locked, whether by pressing the button or by scrolling to the bottom by hand, a glowing pulse emanates from the lock button once, to confirm it. It is a single, brief confirmation in the manner of Apple's own, not a repeating pulse, which would suggest something still going on.
The pulse is in the theme's focus ring colour. A soft, blurred glow blooms around the button, quickly, and fades away. At the same time two thin rings ripple out from the button's centre, the second a moment after the first, each starting as a circle the size of the button and growing to nearly three times that, easing out so it slows as it spreads, thinning and fading to nothing as it goes. All of it is over in under a second. It is drawn over whatever is beside the column, but never takes the mouse.
A list that shows already locked doesn't pulse, and unlocking the scroll while it pulses stops the pulse straight away.

Scrolling the list by hand locks and unlocks it as well: scrolling with the mouse wheel or trackpad over the list, pressing the column's up or down button, or pressing or dragging its thumb. Scrolled by hand to the bottom, the scroll locks there, just as if the button had been pressed. Scrolled by hand away from the bottom while it is locked, the lock breaks straight away, leaving the list wherever it was scrolled to. A list with nothing to scroll keeps its lock as it is. The button stays the way to lock or unlock it wherever the list is: pressing it to lock scrolls the list to the bottom, and pressing it to unlock leaves the list unlocked until it is next scrolled to the bottom by hand.

Completions and auto-imports for the Piton typed into the chat input, and the server the editor's Piton files are edited with.

### LSPShape.server

One `piton lsp` is started as a child process in the selected ProjectDirectoryScope, speaking JSON-RPC over stdio, shared by the chat input and the editor, and restarted whenever the project directory changes. That includes the project opened as the application starts, which gets its server straight away like any other. The client sends `initialize` and `initialized`, answers any request from the server with an empty result, and gives up on a request after 5 seconds. ### LSPShape.stopping

Until then, they work without language support. What the server wrote to its error output before it stopped is logged, with how it stopped. ### LSPShape.document

The server never sees the input's text directly. Results are narrowed to what has been typed of the current word, matches at the start of a name before matches anywhere in it, then ordered by the server's sort text. The hidden anchor's own name is never offered. Accepting a completion inserts it into the input, and the import the server attaches to it (`additionalTextEdits`) is added to the hidden anchor instead of the input.

### LSPShape.autoImport

Names typed by hand are imported with the server's `textDocument/codeAction` quick fixes, repeated up to three times since one import can bring more names into reach. This runs before each completion request and before a prompt is sent.

The completion popup opens at the cursor and is location-aware: it always stays fully inside the window. It opens below the cursor when there is room and above it otherwise, which is the usual case since the input sits at the bottom of the window. It shifts left rather than running past the right edge.
